lines.text: Why is the sky brilliant blue at noon, but shifts into fiery crimson and orange as the sun sets?
The answer is an optical phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering.
Sunlight looks white, but it contains all the colors of the visible rainbow.
Blue light has short, choppy wavelengths that easily scatter in every direction off nitrogen gas molecules at midday.
At sunset, the Sun sits low on the horizon, forcing its rays to travel through ten times more atmosphere to reach your eyes.
Most blue and violet light gets scattered away long before reaching you, leaving only long red and orange wavelengths.
You are seeing the longest light wavelengths making it through the atmosphere's marathon run.
